extracted.intended_audience: Australian Government policy makers and agencies preparing Regulatory Impact Statements (RIS) and developing regulatory consultation processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and conducting consultation as part of Regulatory Impact Statement (RIS) development, covering who to consult, how, timing, accessibility, and how consultation will be assessed by OBPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the purpose and objectives of consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the consultation section of the RIS, you must explain the purpose and objectives of consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State why you are consulting (e.g. to gather ideas, collect evidence, validate assumptions, clarify impacts), what you hope to achieve in each consultation round, and the context for consultation so stakeholders can contribute effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline a plan for conducting consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the consultation section of the RIS, you must outline a plan for conducting consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consultation plan should ideally cover the whole policy making process and identify objectives of consultations, relevant target groups, appropriate forms of consultation and consultation times. Publishing a consultation plan provides stakeholders with early warning and improves transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain who should be consulted—and who does not need to be consulted
rubrics_metrics.description: In the consultation section of the RIS, you must explain who should be consulted—and who does not need to be consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively identify relevant interested parties and those likely to be affected, distinguish between stakeholder sub-groups (e.g. by size, location, nature of operations), and justify exclusions. Use industry associations, small business groups, peak bodies and individual stakeholders appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline a strategy for the most efficient and meaningful consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the consultation section of the RIS, you must outline a strategy for the most efficient and meaningful consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose consultation forms and timing proportionate to the proposal’s impacts, consider joint consultation with other agencies to minimise burden, and select methods (online, face-to-face, written, focus groups) tailored to stakeholder needs and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarise the major topics to be covered and likely issues
rubrics_metrics.description: In the consultation section of the RIS, you must summarise the major topics to be covered and what issues might be raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide summaries in consultation documents so stakeholders can quickly assess relevance; identify assumptions and areas where input is sought to encourage useful responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation must be undertaken before a final decision (RIS requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIS is required to demonstrate that appropriate consultation has been undertaken. The RIS will be assessed as insufficient if no consultation has taken place prior to a final decision, including consultation with other policy makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consultation occurs early enough to influence policy choices; document consultation activity in the RIS as a consultation statement showing how stakeholder input affected options and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect consultation feedback on all genuine and viable options
rubrics_metrics.description: Your RIS should reflect the feedback received on all genuine and viable options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where stakeholders suggest options during consultation, include or discuss them in the RIS. OBPR pays particular attention to whether options suggested during consultation have been included or discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default to full public consultation unless compelling reasons for limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Full public consultation is the appropriate level of consultation for all proposals unless you make a compelling case for a limited form of consultation (such as market sensitivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat full public consultation as the norm; justify targeted, confidential or post-decision consultation with compelling reasons (e.g. national security, commercial-in-confidence, market sensitivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous consultation from earliest possible stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation with key stakeholders should be continuous and should start as early as possible and continue through all stages of the regulatory cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early consultation (including before Early Assessment) helps define problems, objectives and options, identify potential impacts and improve RIS quality. Ongoing engagement helps spot implementation issues and reduce regulatory capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult with other policy makers and regulators to avoid cumulative/overlapping burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy makers must consult with each other to avoid creating cumulative or overlapping regulatory burdens; consult relevant Australian, state/territory and local government agencies and regulators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intergovernmental consultation identifies whether current regimes suffice, overlapping functions, opportunities to streamline regulation, and innovative non-regulatory approaches. Regulators/service delivery agencies should be consulted for implementation and costing information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad-based consultation to capture stakeholder diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: You must consider the scope of proposed regulatory changes and consult widely to capture the diversity of stakeholders affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant groups include the general public, businesses, consumers, unions, environmental groups, state/territory/local governments, and Australian Government entities. Consider subgroup differences (size, operations, location) and engage individuals where peak bodies do not represent all views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible consultation (plain language, appropriate channels, support for disadvantaged stakeholders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation should ensure that your stakeholders can readily contribute to policy development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform stakeholders by appropriate means (e.g. Business Consultation website), use plain language and summaries, post documentation online, consider assistance strategies for those lacking resources, and employ a mix of consultation forms (meetings, focus groups, surveys, web forums). Respond promptly to queries via social media, phones or face-to-face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a range of consultation forms including online and Web 2.0 tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation can take a variety of forms such as stakeholder/public meetings, working groups, focus groups, surveys or web forums (blogs, wikis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online consultations can range from simple websites requesting submissions to interactive use of blogs, wikis, discussion forums, microblogs and social networking sites. Choose tools according to the engagement needed—blogs for announcements/comments, wikis for collaborative drafting, discussion forums for in-depth engagement, microblogs for short alerts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not burdensome: be mindful of stakeholders’ time and capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultations should not make unreasonable demands; timeframes should be realistic to allow considered responses and avoid periods when stakeholders are busy (holidays, end of financial year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider stakeholders’ full-time jobs and business commitments, especially small businesses. Minimise repeated demands by coordinating with other agencies and use joint consultation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent consultation: explain objectives, decision process and how input will be used
rubrics_metrics.description: Involving stakeholders early promotes transparency; you should explain the objectives and context, when/how the final decision will be made, and clearly state aspects that are final and not subject to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make information and draft documents (discussion papers, draft RISs, white/green papers, exposure drafts) available to enable informed comments. Show stakeholders how responses were considered in the RIS and respond to feedback respectfully even if not adopted. Publish relevant documentation online where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent procedures with flexibility for confidentiality where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent consultation procedures aid participation and coordination, but public consultation may be inappropriate in some cases (national security, commercial-in-confidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confidential consultation discreetly and on a case-by-case basis. Consult OBPR early on appropriate level of consultation and alternative approaches when public consultation is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject to evaluation and review: evaluate consultation effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy agencies should evaluate their consultation processes and examine ways to improve effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation can include number/types of responses, which methods were most successful, accessibility promotion, and how consultation clarified options or affected final decisions. OBPR encourages agencies to publish consultation protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not rushed: allow realistic timeframes (usually 30–60 days; minimum 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation rounds should provide enough time for considered responses; depending on significance, 30 to 60 days is usually appropriate with 30 days as the minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer periods may be needed for complex proposals, multiple rounds, or where stakeholders have limited resources (individuals, small businesses). Involving standing consultative bodies in timeline setting can build positive relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation is a means, not an end
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation should be used to improve decisions, not as a substitute for making decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-consult merely for its own sake. Additional consultation is not required as part of the RIS if other appropriate legislative consultation requirements have already been met and are proportionate to the proposal’s magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consultation plans covering objectives, stakeholders, methods and timing per round
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation plans should cover: objectives of each consultation round; who will be consulted in each round; the form of consultation for each round; and when each round will commence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether each round aims to gather ideas, collect evidence, validate assumptions, or clarify impacts. Decide who to consult (broad groups and individuals with technical knowledge), select methods (written, informal early engagement, online forums), and schedule timing (start early; green papers early; exposure drafts closer to finalisation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Release exposure drafts for complex regulations to test implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finalising policy, test the details of complex regulations with relevant businesses by releasing exposure drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure drafts help verify stakeholder understanding of legal application, rights and obligations, and identify simplifications or implementation issues. Use exposure drafts for significant matters to get detailed comments on practical operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: OBPR assessment criteria for consultation in RIS
rubrics_metrics.description: OBPR assesses consultation in the RIS by asking: (1) Does your RIS explain the purpose and objectives of consultation (before the final decision)? (2) Does it have an appropriate plan for consulting those affected by the policy (before the final decision)? (3) Does it demonstrate that the views of affected stakeholder groups have been considered?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Final Assessment OBPR examines whether consultation was transparently described and appropriate at each stage, with attention to whether options suggested during consultation were included or discussed. Lack of appropriate consultation before a final decision may render the RIS insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four consultation types and when each is appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four consultation options: full public, targeted, confidential and post-decision; full public is the default unless compelling reasons exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate uses (from Table 1): Full public — when transparency/public accountability is priority and integrity won't be compromised by early scrutiny. Targeted — when affected stakeholders are in a small or well-defined area/sector and involving unaffected parties would waste effort. Confidential — when sensitivity requires discreet engagement to avoid needless alarm or compromise. Post-decision — when the decision is market-sensitive, consultation before decision would undermine effectiveness, or open consultation serves no useful policy purpose; focus post-decision consultation on implementation, timeframes and reviews.
